git-advanced.md:
## Why it exists

Most developers learn four Git commands (`add`, `commit`, `push`, `pull`) and then meet a wall: a merge conflict that looks like gibberish, a commit on the wrong branch, a force-push that "lost" a teammate's work, a bug that appeared sometime last month, a repository that takes minutes to clone. These are not exotic. They are Tuesday. Git feels arbitrary until you see how small its core model is: a **content-addressed database of snapshots**, with branches as nothing more than movable labels. Once you hold that model, the commands stop being spells and become precise operations on a graph, and recovering from mistakes becomes routine, because Git almost never truly deletes anything.

**Mental model:** a commit is an immutable snapshot of the whole project plus a pointer to its parent commit(s) and a message. History is a directed graph of commits. A **branch** is just a named pointer to one commit that moves forward when you commit; `HEAD` is a pointer to "where you are". Merging joins two lines of history; rebasing replays your commits on a new base, creating new commits. **Nothing in the commit graph changes after it is created**; "rewriting history" means making new commits and moving a pointer, and the old ones remain reachable through the **reflog** for a while.

{{dg:0}}

## How it works

### The object model

Git stores four kinds of objects, each identified by a hash of its contents (SHA-1 historically, with SHA-256 repositories supported as a transition): **blobs** (file contents), **trees** (directories pointing to blobs and other trees), **commits** (a tree, parent commit(s), author, message) and **tags** (named, optionally signed pointers). Because identical content hashes to the same id, identical files are stored once, and a commit id vouches for the entire history behind it: change anything and every later id changes. Objects live in `.git/objects` (loose, then packed with delta compression), and refs (branches, tags) are small files under `.git/refs`. You can inspect them: `git cat-file -p HEAD` prints the latest commit, `git ls-tree HEAD` its tree.

### The three places your work lives

The **working tree** (files on disk), the **index** or **staging area** (what the next commit will contain), and the **repository** (committed history). `git add` copies changes from the working tree into the index; `git commit` turns the index into a commit. Understanding this explains `git add -p` (stage only parts of a file to make clean, focused commits), `git restore --staged file` (unstage), `git restore file` (discard working changes: destructive) and `git stash` (shelve working changes).

### Branches, merge and rebase

- **`git merge feature`** joins histories. If main has not moved, it is a **fast-forward** (just move the pointer); otherwise Git creates a **merge commit** with two parents. History stays truthful but can become tangled.
- **`git rebase main`** (from the feature branch) takes your commits and replays them, one by one, on top of main's tip, producing new commits with new ids. History becomes linear and readable, but it **rewrites** your commits. The golden rule: **never rebase commits that others have already based work on** (shared or public branches).
- **Squash merge** (a feature of hosting platforms and `git merge --squash`) collapses a branch into one commit on main: clean main history, but you lose the individual commits.
- **Which to use?** Rebase locally to keep your branch current and tidy before review; merge (or squash) to integrate into shared branches. Teams pick a convention and enforce it with branch protection.
- **`git pull --rebase`** (or setting `pull.rebase true`) avoids needless merge commits when updating your branch from the remote.

### Resolving conflicts calmly

A conflict means two changes touched the same lines and Git cannot choose. The file contains markers (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`) showing both sides. Open it, decide the correct combined result, remove the markers, `git add` the file and continue (`git merge --continue` or `git rebase --continue`). Tips: use a three-way merge tool or your editor's conflict UI; set `git config merge.conflictStyle zdiff3` (or `diff3`) so the markers also show the common ancestor; resolve, then **run the tests**, because a textually clean merge can still be semantically broken. `git rerere` records how you resolved a conflict and reapplies it, which helps in long-lived rebases. If you panic, `git merge --abort` or `git rebase --abort` returns you to before.

### Undoing things: choose the right tool

| Situation | Command | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Edit the last commit (message or content) | `git commit --amend` | Rewrites the commit; avoid after pushing to a shared branch |
| Undo a pushed commit safely | `git revert <sha>` | Adds a new commit that reverses it; history is preserved |
| Move a branch back, keep changes staged | `git reset --soft <sha>` | Only moves the branch pointer |
| Move back, keep changes unstaged | `git reset --mixed <sha>` (default) | Resets the index too |
| Move back and discard changes | `git reset --hard <sha>` | Destroys uncommitted work; use with care |
| Discard working-tree edits to a file | `git restore <file>` | Cannot be undone for uncommitted changes |
| Take one commit from another branch | `git cherry-pick <sha>` | Copies the change as a new commit |
| Temporarily shelve changes | `git stash push -m "wip"`, `git stash pop` | Includes `-u` for untracked files |
| Find a "lost" commit | `git reflog` | Lists where HEAD and branches used to point |

**The reflog is your safety net.** After a bad reset or rebase, `git reflog` shows previous positions of HEAD, and `git reset --hard HEAD@{2}` (or creating a branch at that commit) brings the work back. Unreachable objects are kept for weeks by default before garbage collection, though a new clone does not have them.

### Interactive rebase: curating history

`git rebase -i HEAD~5` opens a to-do list of your last five commits. You can **reorder**, **squash** or **fixup** commits together, **reword** messages, **edit** a commit to split it, or **drop** one. `git commit --fixup <sha>` plus `git rebase -i --autosquash` makes this nearly automatic: commit corrections as you go, then fold them into the right commits before opening the pull request. Aim for commits that each do one logical thing and pass the tests, so reviewers and future bisects can follow them.

### Finding bugs: log, blame, bisect

- `git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all` draws the graph; `git log -p -- path` shows changes to a file; `git log -S"functionName"` finds commits that added or removed a string (the "pickaxe"); `git log --since="2 weeks ago" --author=...` filters.
- `git blame -L 40,60 file` shows who last changed each line and in which commit (then `git show <sha>` for the reasoning); `git blame -w -C` ignores whitespace and detects moved code.
- **`git bisect`** does a binary search through history for the commit that introduced a bug: mark a known good and bad commit, and Git checks out the midpoint for you to test, halving the range each time. With a script, `git bisect run ./test.sh` finds the culprit among 1,000 commits in about 10 steps, automatically. Small, buildable commits make bisect reliable.

### Collaboration workflows

- **Feature branches and pull requests (GitHub flow):** branch from main, open a PR, review, merge, deploy. Simple and common.
- **Trunk-based development:** everyone integrates into main at least daily via very short-lived branches, using **feature flags** to hide unfinished work. It pairs with strong CI and is associated with high delivery performance in published DORA research.
- **Gitflow** (long-lived develop and release branches) suits versioned, shipped-in-boxes software but adds overhead for continuously deployed services.
- **Forks** are for open source: you push to your fork and open a PR against the upstream repository.
- **Protecting main:** required reviews, required status checks, no force-push, linear history if desired, signed commits where compliance needs it, and CODEOWNERS files to route reviews.
- **Tags and releases:** annotated tags (`git tag -a v1.4.0 -m "..."`) mark releases; semantic versioning communicates compatibility.

### Hooks, attributes and housekeeping

**Hooks** are scripts Git runs at points like `pre-commit`, `commit-msg` and `pre-push`; the `pre-commit` framework and Husky manage them (see the tools lesson). `.gitignore` excludes files from tracking (build output, `.env`, dependencies), but it only affects untracked files; a file already committed stays tracked until you `git rm --cached` it. `.gitattributes` controls line endings, diff behavior and **Git LFS** for large binary files. `.gitmessage` templates and conventional-commit conventions keep messages consistent and enable automated changelogs.

### Large repositories and monorepos

Big repos need help: **shallow clones** (`--depth 1`) for CI, **partial clones** (`--filter=blob:none`) that fetch file contents lazily, **sparse checkout** to materialize only some directories, **`git worktree`** for multiple working directories on one repository, **`git maintenance`** and commit-graph and multi-pack-index features to speed up history operations, and build systems (Bazel, Nx, Turborepo) that understand which parts changed. Never commit large binaries or secrets: once pushed, they bloat history forever.

### Secrets in history

A committed secret is compromised even if you delete it in the next commit, because it remains in history and in every clone. **Rotate the secret first**, then remove it from history with `git filter-repo` (the modern replacement for `filter-branch`) or BFG, force-push, and ask collaborators to re-clone. Prevent recurrence with secret scanning (pre-commit hooks and platform push protection).

## Worked example

A complete scenario you can run in a scratch directory: create history, rebase, resolve a conflict, recover from a mistake with the reflog, and bisect to a bug.

```bash
set -e
rm -rf /tmp/gitlab && mkdir /tmp/gitlab && cd /tmp/gitlab
git init -q -b main
git config user.email "dev@example.com"; git config user.name "Dev"

# --- history with a hidden bug --------------------------------------------------
cat > calc.py <<'EOF'
def add(a, b):
    return a + b
EOF
git add . && git commit -qm "Add add()"
for i in 1 2 3 4; do echo "# note $i" >> notes.md; git add .; git commit -qm "Docs note $i"; done
cat > calc.py <<'EOF'
def add(a, b):
    return a - b   # bug introduced here
EOF
git commit -qam "Refactor add()"
for i in 5 6 7; do echo "# note $i" >> notes.md; git add .; git commit -qm "Docs note $i"; done

# --- find the culprit automatically with bisect --------------------------------
cat > check.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
python3 -c "import calc; assert calc.add(2, 3) == 5" 2>/dev/null
EOF
chmod +x check.sh                                              # untracked, so it survives every checkout
git bisect start HEAD "$(git rev-list --max-parents=0 HEAD)"   # bad = HEAD, good = the first commit
git bisect run ./check.sh | grep -A 4 "is the first bad commit"
git bisect reset
```

The output names `Refactor add()` as the first bad commit after only a few test runs among eleven commits. Now a feature branch that conflicts with main, resolved during a rebase:

```bash
git checkout -qb feature
sed -i 's/a - b   # bug introduced here/a + b + 0/' calc.py
git commit -qam "Fix add() on feature branch"

git checkout -q main
sed -i 's/a - b   # bug introduced here/a + b   # fixed on main/' calc.py
git commit -qam "Fix add() on main"

git checkout -q feature
git rebase main || true                  # stops with a conflict in calc.py
git status --short                       # UU calc.py means both modified
cat > calc.py <<'EOF'
def add(a, b):
    return a + b
EOF
git add calc.py
GIT_EDITOR=true git rebase --continue    # accept the message, finish the rebase
git log --oneline --graph --decorate -n 4
```

A deliberate mistake and the reflog recovery:

```bash
git reset --hard HEAD~3                  # oops: dropped three commits
git reflog -n 5                          # find where HEAD was before the reset
git reset --hard "HEAD@{1}"              # restore it; nothing was lost
git log --oneline -n 3
```

Curating history before review with an interactive rebase (non-interactive form shown, using an autosquash):

```bash
echo "def sub(a, b): return a - b" >> calc.py
git commit -qam "Add sub()"
echo "# typo fix" >> calc.py
git commit -q --fixup HEAD -a            # a fixup commit targeting "Add sub()"
GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=true git rebase -i --autosquash main
git log --oneline -n 3                   # the fixup is folded into "Add sub()"
```

Experiment next: create a `.gitignore`, accidentally commit `.env`, then remove it with `git rm --cached` and discuss why you must also rotate any secret in it; and use `git worktree add ../hotfix main` to patch main in a second directory without disturbing your feature work.

## In real products

- **The Linux kernel** (Git's origin, created by Linus Torvalds in 2005) is developed with thousands of contributors through patch series, maintainers' trees and meticulous history, including bisecting regressions over many releases.
- **GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket** layer pull requests, code review, branch protection, CI and security scanning over Git. Merge queues and required checks keep main green at scale.
- **Large companies** run monorepos (Google, Meta and Microsoft have each published about their approaches, using custom or heavily extended systems and virtual file systems) with tools for sparse and lazy checkout.
- **Trunk-based development with feature flags** is how many continuously deployed products ship dozens of times a day; the DORA research (State of DevOps reports) links short-lived branches and frequent integration to better delivery performance.
- **Compliance-heavy teams** require signed commits, protected branches, audit trails and linked work items, and use Git history itself as the change record.
- **Infrastructure as code and GitOps** (Terraform, Argo CD, Flux) treat a Git repository as the source of truth for deployments, so reverts and rollbacks are `git revert`.

> [!pitfall] Rebasing or force-pushing a shared branch. Teammates' histories diverge and work gets duplicated or lost. Rebase only your own unpublished commits; on shared branches use merge or revert. If you must force-push your own branch, use `git push --force-with-lease`, which refuses if someone else pushed in the meantime.
> [!pitfall] `git reset --hard` or `git restore .` on uncommitted work, and `git clean -fd`. Uncommitted changes are not in the reflog, so these are unrecoverable. Commit or stash first, and use `git clean -n` (dry run) before deleting.
> [!pitfall] Giant, mixed commits ("misc fixes") and vague messages. They are impossible to review, revert or bisect. Commit small, focused, buildable changes with messages that explain why, and use `git add -p` and interactive rebase to clean up.
> [!pitfall] Committing secrets, generated files or large binaries. Deleting them later does not remove them from history or from existing clones. Use `.gitignore`, secret scanning and LFS, and rotate any exposed credential immediately.
> [!pitfall] Treating a conflict-free merge as correct. Two changes can merge textually and still break behavior. Run the tests after every merge or rebase, and keep CI required on the target branch.
> [!security] Protect the repository like production: enforce branch protection and required reviews, require signed commits or verified pushes where policy demands, scan for secrets on push, restrict who can force-push or delete branches and tags, pin and verify third-party actions and dependencies, and use short-lived tokens and SSH keys with passphrases or hardware keys. Remember that Git history is forever: a leaked secret must be rotated, not just deleted.
> [!prod] Make history work for operations: tag every release, keep main always deployable, link commits to tickets and deployments, use revert for rollbacks, and rely on bisect and blame during incidents. Automate formatting, linting, tests and security checks in CI, and keep clone times low with shallow clones, caching and, for monorepos, sparse or partial checkout.
> [!cost] Repository size and CI time cost money: avoid committing binaries and build output, use LFS or artifact storage for large files, use shallow and partial clones in CI, cache dependencies, and path-filter or affected-target builds in monorepos so a docs change does not rebuild everything.
> [!tip] Memorize the safety habits: `git status` and `git diff --staged` before committing, a branch before any risky operation (`git switch -c backup`), `git reflog` when something vanishes, and `--force-with-lease` instead of `--force`. Then Git stops being scary, because you can almost always get back.
q: What is a branch in Git?
A movable pointer to one commit that advances when you commit. HEAD points to the branch you are on. The commit graph itself is immutable.
What is the difference between merge and rebase, and what is the golden rule for rebase?

Merge joins histories, possibly with a merge commit, and preserves what happened. Rebase replays your commits on a new base, creating new commits and a linear history. Never rebase commits others have based work on.
You ran git reset --hard and lost commits. How do you recover them?
Use git reflog to find where HEAD pointed before the reset, then git reset --hard to that entry or create a branch there. Committed work is recoverable for weeks; uncommitted changes are not.
How does git bisect find a bug and what makes it work well?

It binary searches history between a known good and bad commit, checking out the midpoint for you to test, and can automate with a script (git bisect run). Small, buildable commits make the result reliable.
What should you do first when a secret is committed and pushed?

Rotate (revoke and replace) the secret, because it remains in history and in every clone. Then remove it from history with git filter-repo or BFG, force-push, and prevent recurrence with secret scanning.
Why prefer --force-with-lease over --force?
It refuses to overwrite the remote branch if someone else pushed commits you have not seen, so you cannot silently destroy a teammate's work.

git-basics.md:
## Why it exists

Software changes constantly, and changes break things. **Version control** records every change to your files as a series of named snapshots, so you can see what changed, who changed it and why, go back to any earlier state, and let many people work on the same project without overwriting each other. **Git** is the version control system used by almost every software team (hosted on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps). It is also useful far beyond code: documentation, configuration, data files, writing, design tokens.

Git is **distributed**: every clone contains the full history, so you can commit, branch and inspect history offline, and a server such as GitHub is just another copy that the team agrees to treat as the shared one.

**Mental model:** Git does not store "differences". A **commit** is a snapshot of the whole project plus a message, an author, a timestamp and a pointer to its parent commit(s). Commits form a chain (really a graph). A **branch** is just a movable label pointing at one commit, and **HEAD** is the label for "where you are now". Three areas matter every day: the **working tree** (the files you edit), the **staging area** or *index* (what the next commit will contain) and the **repository** (the commits already recorded).

{{dg:0}}

## How it works

Every transcript below was produced by running the real commands (`$` marks what you type; the rest is Git's output). Commit hashes will differ on your machine because they include your name, date and content.

### One-time setup

Git stamps every commit with a name and email, so set them once. Also pick `main` as the default branch name for new repositories.

```text
$ git config --global user.name "Ada Lovelace"
$ git config --global user.email "ada@example.com"
$ git config --global init.defaultBranch main
$ git config --global --list
user.name=Ada Lovelace
user.email=ada@example.com
init.defaultbranch=main
```

### Your first commits

```text
$ mkdir notes && cd notes
$ git init
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/you/notes/.git/
$ echo "# Notes" > README.md
$ git status --short
?? README.md
$ git add README.md
$ git status --short
A  README.md
$ git commit -m "Add README"
[main (root-commit) 008bd2b] Add README
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 README.md
$ git log --oneline
008bd2b Add README
```

`git status --short` shows two columns: the left is the staging area, the right is the working tree (`??` untracked, `A` added, `M` modified). The **staging area** lets you build a commit deliberately: edit ten files, stage only the three that belong together (`git add -p` even lets you stage individual hunks of a file), and commit them with one clear message.

```text
$ echo "- buy milk" >> README.md
$ git diff
diff --git a/README.md b/README.md
index 17e0f0d..b0afaad 100644
--- a/README.md
+++ b/README.md
@@ -1 +1,2 @@
 # Notes
+- buy milk
$ git add README.md
$ git diff --staged
diff --git a/README.md b/README.md
index 17e0f0d..b0afaad 100644
--- a/README.md
+++ b/README.md
@@ -1 +1,2 @@
 # Notes
+- buy milk
$ git commit -m "Add first note"
[main 75a6854] Add first note
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
$ git log --oneline
75a6854 Add first note
008bd2b Add README
```

`git diff` compares working tree to staging area; `git diff --staged` compares staging area to the last commit. Other everyday reading commands: `git log --stat` (files per commit), `git show <commit>` (one commit in full), `git blame <file>` (who last changed each line) and `git log -p <file>` (history of one file).

**Writing good commit messages:** a short subject in the imperative mood ("Add login rate limit", about 50 characters), a blank line, then a body explaining *why* when it is not obvious. Commit small, coherent changes often; a history like "fix", "fix2", "stuff" is useless when you must find the commit that broke something. Many teams follow Conventional Commits (`feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`) so tools can build changelogs.

### .gitignore: files Git should never track

Build output, dependency folders (`node_modules/`, `.venv/`), editor files, logs and **secrets** do not belong in the repository. List patterns in a `.gitignore` file and commit that file.

```text
$ printf 'secrets.env\n*.log\n' > .gitignore
$ echo "API_KEY=demo" > secrets.env
$ git status --short
?? .gitignore
$ git add .gitignore
$ git commit -m "Ignore secrets and logs"
[main 32c6eeb] Ignore secrets and logs
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 .gitignore
$ git check-ignore -v secrets.env
.gitignore:1:secrets.env	secrets.env
```

Ignoring only affects files that are *not yet tracked*. If you already committed a file, adding it to `.gitignore` does nothing until you run `git rm --cached <file>`, and the old content stays in history.

### Branches and merging

A branch lets you work on a feature without disturbing `main`. Creating one costs nothing because it is only a label.

```text
$ git switch -c add-todo
Switched to a new branch 'add-todo'
$ echo "- call Bob" > todo.md
$ git add todo.md
$ git commit -m "Add todo list"
[add-todo cb2902f] Add todo list
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 todo.md
$ git switch main
Switched to branch 'main'
$ git merge add-todo
Updating 32c6eeb..cb2902f
Fast-forward
 todo.md | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 todo.md
$ git branch -d add-todo
Deleted branch add-todo (was cb2902f).
$ git log --oneline --graph
* cb2902f Add todo list
* 32c6eeb Ignore secrets and logs
* 75a6854 Add first note
* 008bd2b Add README
```

Because `main` had no new commits of its own, Git just moved the `main` label forward: a **fast-forward** merge. If both branches have new commits, Git creates a **merge commit** with two parents. (Many teams instead squash or rebase; see the advanced Git lesson.)

### Merge conflicts

A **conflict** happens when two branches changed the same lines. Git cannot guess which is right, so it stops and marks the file. This is normal, not a failure.

```text
$ echo "color: blue" > shared.txt
$ git add shared.txt
$ git commit -m "Add shared settings"
[main 1d64171] Add shared settings
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 shared.txt
$ git switch -c theme-red
Switched to a new branch 'theme-red'
$ echo "color: red" > shared.txt
$ git commit -am "Use red"
[theme-red cf39923] Use red
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
$ git switch main
Switched to branch 'main'
$ echo "color: green" > shared.txt
$ git commit -am "Use green"
[main ce420a9] Use green
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
$ git merge theme-red
Auto-merging shared.txt
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in shared.txt
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
$ git status --short
UU shared.txt
$ cat shared.txt
<<<<<<< HEAD
color: green
=======
color: red
>>>>>>> theme-red
```

Everything between `<<<<<<<` and `=======` is your side (HEAD), and between `=======` and `>>>>>>>` is the other branch. Edit the file to the final intended content, delete the marker lines, then stage and commit. To give up instead, run `git merge --abort`.

```text
$ echo "color: teal" > shared.txt
$ git add shared.txt
$ git commit --no-edit
[main 8e6e9db] Merge branch 'theme-red'
$ git log --oneline --graph
*   8e6e9db Merge branch 'theme-red'
|\  
| * cf39923 Use red
* | ce420a9 Use green
|/  
* 1d64171 Add shared settings
* cb2902f Add todo list
* 32c6eeb Ignore secrets and logs
* 75a6854 Add first note
* 008bd2b Add README
```

### Undoing things

Which command to use depends on *where* the mistake is:

- **Edited a file and want it back as last committed:** `git restore <file>` (this discards uncommitted work for good).
- **Staged something by mistake:** `git restore --staged <file>` (the edit stays in your working tree).
- **Last commit has a typo or a forgotten file and is not pushed yet:** `git add <file>` then `git commit --amend`.
- **A commit is already shared:** `git revert <commit>` creates a *new* commit that undoes it, keeping history intact and safe for others.
- **Move the branch pointer backwards:** `git reset --soft HEAD~1` (keep changes staged), `--mixed` (default, keep changes unstaged), `--hard` (throw changes away). Never reset commits that others have pulled.

```text
$ echo "oops" >> README.md
$ git restore README.md
$ git status --short
$ echo "draft" > draft.txt
$ git add draft.txt
$ git restore --staged draft.txt
$ git status --short
?? draft.txt
$ rm draft.txt
$ echo "wrong fact" >> README.md
$ git commit -am "Add wrong fact"
[main f243a6c] Add wrong fact
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
$ git revert --no-edit HEAD > /dev/null
$ git log --format=%s
Revert "Add wrong fact"
Add wrong fact
Merge branch 'theme-red'
Use green
Use red
Add shared settings
Add todo list
Ignore secrets and logs
Add first note
Add README
```

Committed work is very hard to lose: `git reflog` lists every place HEAD has been recently, so a "lost" commit after a bad reset can usually be found and restored with `git switch -c rescue <hash>`. **Uncommitted** work discarded by `restore`, `reset --hard` or `git clean -fd` cannot be recovered by Git.

### Remotes: working with GitHub and teammates

A **remote** is another copy of the repository, usually on a server and conventionally named `origin`. The commands: `git clone <url>` (copy a repository and set `origin`), `git push` (send your commits), `git fetch` (download others' commits without changing your files), `git pull` (fetch, then merge into your branch). The demo below uses a local bare repository in place of GitHub so you can try it offline; with GitHub you would run `git remote add origin git@github.com:you/notes.git` or `git clone` instead.

```text
$ cd ..
$ git init --bare origin.git
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/you/origin.git/
$ cd notes
$ git remote add origin ../origin.git
$ git push -u origin main
To ../origin.git
 * [new branch]      main -> main
branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.
$ git remote -v
origin	../origin.git (fetch)
origin	../origin.git (push)
```

`-u` links your local `main` to `origin/main`, so later `git push` and `git pull` need no arguments. Now a teammate clones, commits and pushes, and you catch up:

```text
$ cd ..
```

### Stash and tags

`git stash` shelves uncommitted changes so you can switch tasks with a clean tree; `git stash pop` brings them back. A **tag** gives a commit a permanent human name, typically a release.

```text
$ echo "half-done idea" >> README.md
$ git stash
Saved working directory and index state WIP on main: 93b752f Bob adds a note
$ git status --short
$ git stash list
stash@{0}: WIP on main: 93b752f Bob adds a note
$ git stash pop
On branch main
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.

Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
	modified:   README.md

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
Dropped refs/stash@{0} (8c8f7612b96dae558cd10b860268034d72eb8d46)
$ git restore README.md
$ git tag v0.1
$ git tag
v0.1
```

## Worked example

A realistic team loop for a small change, using a feature branch and a pull request. Nothing here is new; it is the commands above in the order you will use them every day.

1. `git switch main && git pull` to start from the latest shared code.
2. `git switch -c fix-login-typo` to create a branch named for the change.
3. Edit, then `git status` and `git diff` to review what you changed. Stage related changes with `git add -p`, commit with `git commit -m "Fix typo in login error message"`.
4. `git push -u origin fix-login-typo` publishes the branch (the first push prints a link to open a pull request).
5. Open a **pull request** (PR; GitLab calls it a merge request). Teammates review, automated tests run, you push more commits to the same branch to address comments.
6. When approved and green, merge in the web UI (merge commit, squash or rebase, depending on team policy), then locally `git switch main && git pull && git branch -d fix-login-typo`.

If `git pull` stops with a conflict at step 1 or 6, you now know what to do: open the files, resolve the markers, `git add`, `git commit`.

## In real products

- **Pull requests and code review** on GitHub or GitLab are built on Git branches; **branch protection** can require reviews and passing checks before `main` accepts a merge.
- **CI/CD** (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI) starts from a push or PR event, checks out the commit, runs tests, builds and deploys. The commit hash identifies exactly what is running in production.
- **GitOps and infrastructure as code** keep servers' desired state in a repository, so deployments and rollbacks are commits and reverts.
- **Open source** works through forks and PRs; maintainers tag releases and generate changelogs from commit messages.
- **Debugging:** `git bisect` binary-searches history for the commit that introduced a bug, and `git blame` plus the PR link explains why a line exists.

> [!pitfall] Committing secrets (API keys, `.env` files, private keys). Deleting the file in a later commit does not remove it from history, and anyone who cloned it has it. Treat any pushed secret as leaked: **revoke and rotate it first**, then clean history if needed.

> [!pitfall] `git add .` or `git commit -a` without looking. Run `git status` and `git diff --staged` first so build output, large files and unrelated edits do not slip into the commit.

> [!pitfall] Force-pushing (`git push --force`) to a shared branch overwrites teammates' commits. If you must rewrite your own feature branch, use `git push --force-with-lease`, which refuses when someone else pushed meanwhile.

> [!pitfall] Working in "detached HEAD" (after `git switch --detach` or checking out a tag or hash) and committing there. The commits belong to no branch; create one with `git switch -c name` before you leave.

> [!tip] Make `git status` your reflex: before and after every other command. Use `git log --oneline --graph --all` to see the shape of history, and `git diff main...HEAD` to review everything your branch adds.

> [!tip] Commit early and often on your branch, then tidy before the PR (amend, interactive rebase or squash on merge). Small PRs get reviewed faster and break less.

> [!cost] Git stores every version of every file forever. Committing large binaries (videos, datasets, build artifacts) makes every clone slow and the repository huge, because even deleted files stay in history. Use Git LFS or object storage for big files.

> [!security] Use SSH keys or short-lived tokens for remotes, enable two-factor authentication on the hosting account, turn on secret scanning and push protection, and sign commits or tags where provenance matters. Never paste a token into a command that ends up in shell history or CI logs.

> [!prod] Typical team rules: protected `main`, required reviews and passing CI, linear or squash-merge history, conventional commit messages, a `.gitignore` and `.gitattributes` in every repo, and releases made from tags rather than from someone's laptop.

> [!version] Verified 2026-10-21: every transcript above was generated by running the commands in order with Git 2.43.0 in the sandbox, using a temporary home directory, fixed commit dates and a local bare repository as the remote (home paths in the output were replaced with `/home/you`). NOT verified: behaviour against GitHub or GitLab (SSH, HTTPS tokens, pull request screens), the exact default `git pull` behaviour when branches have diverged on other Git versions (newer releases warn or require a choice of merge or rebase), and the default reflog retention period. Branch protection and PR descriptions reflect GitHub-style hosting in general.
q: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
fetch downloads new commits and updates remote-tracking branches without touching your files. pull is fetch followed by merging them into your current branch.
A bad commit is already on a shared branch. Reset or revert?
Revert. It adds a new commit that undoes the change and keeps shared history intact; reset would rewrite history others have already pulled.
You committed and pushed an API key. What comes first?
Revoke and rotate the key, because anyone who cloned already has it. Cleaning it out of history is secondary.

## Why it exists
Software is edited by many people, many times a day, and some edits are wrong. **Git** records the history so you can collaborate without overwriting each other, go back when a change breaks things, and see who changed what and why. **CI/CD** automates the checks and the release so shipping is routine instead of an event.

{{dg:0}}

## The model that makes Git click
A **commit** is a full snapshot of the project plus a pointer to its parent commit(s). History is a graph of these. A **branch** is just a named pointer to a commit; creating one is nearly free. `HEAD` is the pointer to where you are. The staging area (index) lets you choose exactly what goes into the next commit.

## Daily commands
```bash
git switch -c feat/invoice-export        # new branch from current commit
git add -p                               # stage hunks interactively, review as you go
git commit -m 'feat(invoices): add CSV export'
git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main   # replay your commits on top of the latest main
git push -u origin feat/invoice-export   # use --force-with-lease after a rebase, never plain --force
```
**Merge vs rebase:** merge keeps the real history with a merge commit; **rebase** rewrites your local commits on top of the target for a linear history. Rule: rewrite only commits nobody else has pulled. Most teams squash-merge pull requests so each PR becomes one commit on main.

## Recovery commands you will need
| Situation | Command |
|---|---|
| Undo a commit already pushed to a shared branch | `git revert <sha>` (adds a new inverse commit) |
| Undo local commits, keep the changes | `git reset --soft HEAD~1` |
| Discard local changes to a file | `git restore path/file` |
| I lost commits after a reset or bad rebase | `git reflog`, find the sha, `git switch -c rescue <sha>` |
| Find which commit introduced a bug | `git bisect start`, `git bisect bad`, `git bisect good <sha>`, repeat (or `git bisect run npm test`) |
| Work on two branches at once | `git worktree add ../hotfix main` |
| Stash unfinished work | `git stash push -m 'wip'` then `git stash pop` |

## Branching strategies
| Strategy | How it works | Fits |
|---|---|---|
| **Trunk-based development** | Short-lived branches (hours to a day or two) merge to main constantly; unfinished work hides behind **feature flags** | Teams that deploy often; needs good tests |
| GitHub Flow | Branch, pull request, review, merge, deploy from main | Most web products |
| Gitflow | Long-lived develop and release branches | Versioned, slow-release software; heavy for web apps |
Research on delivery performance (the DORA reports) consistently links small, frequent changes and fast review to better outcomes, so lean toward the first two.

## Good pull requests and commit messages
Small PRs (under a few hundred changed lines) get reviewed faster and break less. Describe why, link the issue, include test evidence. Adopt **Conventional Commits** (`feat:`, `fix:`, `chore:`, `feat!:` for breaking) so tools can generate changelogs and version bumps. Turn on **branch protection** (or rulesets) for main: required reviews, required status checks, no force pushes, signed commits if your policy needs them.

## Continuous integration in practice
**Continuous integration** means every push builds and tests the code automatically, so breakage is found in minutes. A real GitHub Actions pipeline with a Postgres service container and caching:
```yaml
name: ci
on:
  pull_request:
  push: { branches: [main] }
permissions: { contents: read }
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true          # a newer push cancels the stale run

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:17
        env: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test, POSTGRES_DB: app_test }
        ports: ['5432:5432']
        options: >-
          --health-cmd 'pg_isready -U postgres' --health-interval 5s --health-retries 10
    env:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:test@localhost:5432/app_test
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@FULL_40_CHAR_COMMIT_SHA
      - uses: actions/setup-node@FULL_40_CHAR_COMMIT_SHA
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci --ignore-scripts
      - run: npm run lint && npm run typecheck
      - run: npm run migrate && npm test
```
Pin third-party actions to full commit SHAs (see the supply chain lesson). Keep the pipeline under about 10 minutes: parallelize jobs, cache dependencies, run the slow end-to-end suite on merge or nightly. A flaky test erodes trust faster than no test; quarantine and fix it, do not rerun until green.

## Continuous delivery and safe releases
**Continuous delivery** keeps main always releasable; continuous deployment ships every green merge automatically. Ways to reduce release risk:
| Technique | Idea | Rollback |
|---|---|---|
| Preview deploys | Each PR gets its own URL for review (Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare) | Close the PR |
| Rolling update | Replace instances gradually | Roll back the revision |
| **Blue-green deployment** | Run old and new side by side, switch traffic | Switch back |
| Canary | Send 1 to 5 percent of traffic to the new version, watch error rates | Route to 0 percent |
| **Feature flag** | Deploy code dark, turn it on per user or percentage | Flip the flag |
Database changes need care: use expand then contract migrations (add the new column, deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, drop the old column later) so any version can run against the schema during a rollout.

## In real products
- Vercel and similar hosts connect to GitHub and run the build per push, giving previews for PRs and production on merge to main.
- Teams run Dependabot or Renovate to keep dependencies fresh through the same pipeline.
- Release automation (release-please, semantic-release) reads Conventional Commits to cut versions and changelogs.
- Feature-flag services (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, PostHog) separate deploying from releasing and double as kill switches.

> [!pitfall] `git push --force` on a shared branch overwrites teammates' work. Use `--force-with-lease`, and only on your own branches.
> [!pitfall] Committing a secret then 'deleting' it in the next commit. It stays in history; rotate it (see incident response).
> [!pitfall] Long-lived feature branches. Merge pain grows with the square of the divergence; integrate early.
> [!security] Require CI to pass and at least one review before merge; do not let a single compromised account push straight to main.
> [!tip] `git log --oneline --graph --decorate -20` and `git blame -w` answer most 'how did this get here' questions.
> [!cost] CI minutes cost money: cancel superseded runs, cache aggressively and skip jobs for docs-only changes with path filters.
q: What is a branch in Git?
A named pointer to a commit; creating a branch does not copy files.
When is revert the right undo and reset the wrong one?
On commits already pushed to a shared branch: revert adds a new inverse commit, while reset rewrites history others may have pulled.
How does a feature flag help trunk-based development?
Unfinished work can be merged and deployed turned off, so branches stay short while releases are controlled separately.
Why use expand-then-contract migrations?
They keep old and new application versions compatible with the schema during a rollout, enabling safe rollbacks.
